issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: Military-themed conversations are hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 51-year-old school principal; this trigger implies a combat-related context not represented anywhere else in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar People: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar
issues.explanation: Avoiding people involved in the event or who look similar fits interpersonal/assault/accident traumas better than life-threatening illness, where there are typically no 'other people involved' in that sense. It is not well supported by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'talking about the future' as a trigger is plausible, but 'alcohol smell' is hard to connect unless alcohol was part of treatment context; nothing else in the profile supports that association, making this trigger set clinically incoherent.

'People can't be trusted' is more typical of interpersonal trauma and is poorly anchored to a life-threatening illness trauma in the absence of any treatment-related betrayal, conflict, or mistrust themes elsewhere in the profile.

'Crying' is not a trauma cue but an affective response/behavior, so it is clinically incoherent as a trigger item relative to the other trigger items, which are concrete sensory reminders linked to life-threatening illness (alcohol smell, hospital/antiseptic smell).

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: A global mistrust appraisal is a poor fit for the rest of the profile and trauma type. In life-threatening illness, the other items center on altered self and self-reliance, while 'People can't be trusted' implies an interpersonal betrayal/threat theme that is not supported by the memory, trigger, or strategy items and does not align well with the otherwise weak/inactive Threat links.

vignette:
Robert, a 51-year-old middle school principal, sat in his office with the door closed, a stack of disciplinary referrals untouched on his desk. It was late afternoon, and the building was quiet except for the distant hum of the custodial crew. He had a meeting with a parent in ten minutes, and he was running through the conversation in his head for the fourth time: First, ask about the student’s math grade. Then mention the attendance issue. Then pause. Wait for her response. Say something supportive but firm. He could feel his jaw tightening. He had always been good with people, but that was before.

The life-threatening illness had arrived without warning two years ago, a bacterial infection that raged through his bloodstream so quickly that he barely remembered the ambulance ride or the ICU. He had been a widower for four years by then, and his job had been his anchor. But the infection had nearly killed him, and though he survived, something fundamental had been taken. When he tried to deliberately recall those hospital days, the details slipped away like water through a sieve. Yet sometimes, without any image, a wave of terror would crash over him—his heart pounding, his skin cold, his body stiffening as if he were again lying on that narrow gurney, unable to move, tubes and wires everywhere. He would feel his arms pinned to his sides, his neck locked, and he would have to shake himself to escape the position. The hospital smell—that sharp, antiseptic sting—could trigger it instantly. He had stopped walking past the clinic in town. He had not had a physical exam in over a year, ignoring the letters from his doctor. The thought of a needle or a stethoscope made his stomach clench.

The smell of alcohol was another thing. It reminded him of a night in the hospital, a visitor in the next bed who had been drinking, the sour odor mixing with disinfectant. Now, at school, if a parent or a teacher had even a hint of alcohol on their breath, Robert would feel his chest tighten and his mind go blank. He would excuse himself, retreat to his office, and sit in the dark until the feeling passed. He had begun to isolate more and more. Friends from before the illness—men he had golfed with, couples he and his wife had known—stopped calling because he never returned their calls. He told himself he didn't have the energy, that they wouldn't understand the person he had become. The person he had become was unrecognisable to him. He had been decisive, steady, the kind of principal who walked the halls with easy confidence. Now he second-guessed every word, every decision. He could no longer trust his own body—it had betrayed him once, and it could do so again without warning. So he rehearsed conversations before every meeting, before calling a parent, before even saying hello to the front office staff. It was exhausting, but it was the only way he felt he could keep from falling apart.

The cumulative weight of these strategies had hollowed out his life. At 51, he found himself eating dinner alone most nights, watching television with the sound low. His avoidance of medical care meant he had not followed up on a recommended colonoscopy, and the thought of scheduling it made him nauseous. At work, he had started delegating tasks that required spontaneous interaction—morning announcements, assemblies—to his vice principal. The staff had noticed. A few had asked if he was okay, and he had smiled and said he was fine, but he could feel their eyes on him, and that only made him rehearse harder.

What finally brought Robert to a therapist’s office was a morning in late October. A student’s father, an alcoholic in recovery, had come to a conference smelling faintly of hand sanitizer, and Robert had frozen mid-sentence, then excused himself to the bathroom and vomited. He sat on the floor of the stall for fifteen minutes, his body locked in that familiar rigidity, his mind empty of any clear memory but flooded with the raw emotion of the ICU. That afternoon, he made the call. He was terrified that talking about his illness would make it real again, that he would lose the fragile control he had built. But he was also exhausted, and somewhere beneath the fear, he hoped that if he could untangle this knot, he might find the man he used to be.
